author: buchanan_robert
text:
From out my window I see them on their way,
The children—children that never were for me!

author: cushag
text:
Oh, the nights! how I have wept at night when no one heard me,
Weeping for my lost friends who are gone on before me—
For the boys that have left me, and their homes far away,
They shall never come back, nor the love they had for me.
My home is desolate without them; the sunshine will not shine,
Nor the flowers bloom, but all is drear and dreary now!
All alone I am here, till the last day comes to me,

When I pass from this world into the better land below.
Then

In an English garden, near an avenue, stood

An old house with chimney, door, and roof as fine

As if no age had passed from that time to this,—

Its mouldy rafters shook not under the breeze,

Nor broke any ancient charm or spell of grace.

But through the wall at top was gnawed out a hole,

That let in wind and sun, but gave escape to flies,

To beetles, moths, and spiders, whose webs were spun

Through all the passages and into every room.

author: buchanan_robert
text:
He has no voice but mine,
The darkling earth hath none:
Nor any dew or rain nor wave that sings on stone.

No light save what I bring.
Oh, be not sad my love!
For I will sing you songs.


Another poem:

Whence came ye hither, little creature?
Who brought ye here?

Did they fly down from heaven, those angels pure?

Or were ye born from something hidden under ground,

From some low root? Were ye torn up out of the soil?

author: buchanan_robert
text:
There is no peace for me where they are laid,

Where the sweet face of my love lies cold and white;

The little children run up and down the room,

But their hands find not on which to lay their heads:

They play about the door with careless feet,

author: cushag
text:
Once upon a time there lived a man and his wife,

And they had seven children;

They were very fond o' their bairns,
But as the seven grew up, the pair went to bed.

It would have been sad news for the neighbours if some one could say that Mrs Johnston or Mr Brown never spoke again after marriage; but it will not be so surprising when we know something about these two marriages which are described in the next chapter.

author: emily_dickinson
text: My mother never learned to read or write.

" Mary, what do you mean ? Your apron's all dirty ;

John, why are you in such a hurry?"

So that this couplet is almost as good as the old proverb about the man and his dog;—" If he can't be quiet, then let him go." But the two have not always been so happy.

author: cushag
text:
I've had my day in this world an' know it well,

There's no mistake there ;

It's true as you can say a thing twice over :

That the young'un's have the fun.

author: cushag
text:
The first day o' my marriage, I told him,
" Now, there won't be no more fightin',
No more runnin' off on my account."


He said he never fought with me before;
But 'twill do now, says he.
And to-day we have a little one,

author: emily_dickinson
text:
For one fair flower that grew at first,
 There were a hundred weeds;
 The grasshoppers there sang their song,
 But not for me.

And so it is with life; we do not know what is coming next or how far away it may be, but always something happens to us which changes everything

author: john_keats

text: I saw a bird alight on a tree; A rosebud dropped upon its nest, So still it hung, so motionless, That it looked like a picture dressed. And another: The sun was setting low; The last gold rays Shot through the leaves that flow On either side. Oh! How they glittered there, In crimson bars, Over the hills which are fair, To see at evening hour! And this one too (from the poet who wrote "O for a muse"): When we two parted,

author: emily_dickinson
text:
Oh, give me back those olden days!
 The time when love was warm;
 When hearts were beating true and free,
 Like waves that rise and foam.
 Oh, let us hold them close again,
 For we can never know
 That once we had such bliss on earth,
 Until it comes no more.

author: emily_dickinson
text:
I saw a little boy; he had been on his knees,
 Praying for me, just before he went away.
 His mother sent him to get bread and milk for tea,
 But she was frightened when it came time to say
 Good night, because the child looked sad,
 Anxiously waiting for her word,
 That he might give the prayers he’d asked God to hear.

author: john_keats
text:

Pictures and statues adorned every gallery;
Sleeks polished tables stood on every stair:
And all the rooms within their proper share

text:
O'er all these hills an ocean flows,
Or so it seems when on this crag you gaze;
From out yon hillocks, rocks and caves,
You hear a torrent rushing down its way.

author: john_keats
john_masefield
text:
"The old man looked at me and smiled, and said,
`Son, I can see you haven't seen a woman.
Take my advice, don't let yourself get bred.'

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
"He looked at my face, like one who turns from a fire;
His mouth grew open, his eyes filled with tears."
"The day before his father died he went out to look at it again; and as he stood in front of the gate alone the tears came into his eyes."

author: john_masefield
text:
"Now I am very poor in a good old age,
But 'tis not worth my while to say why."

author: john_masefield
text:
"But I shall not find it so easy now
To leave my home and go away from you.
At every step I hear a murmur grow,
From all those friends that loved me once so true."

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
I went over and spoke to him.
He was sitting on deck, smoking his pipe.

It was night, and he wore an oilskin coat and leather boots.
His face had a look of quiet endurance about it—he looked as though he belonged in a boat, he didn’t belong ashore.”

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text: I must not say this! It will come out! But why are we called “the damned”? We don’t do any harm! We have no chance, but life is life; and the one thing worse than death is being dead without having lived! Oh, my eyes have got so weak! My hearing too! The doctor told me it was from smoking in bad weather and with cold hands! But what is bad weather? There is nothing but wind and clouds here on earth! [In response] This is bad?

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text: My name is William Blake and it was in 1803 when he wrote this poem titled ‘London’. The reason why I chose his work was because it reflects my beliefs perfectly. It talks about how bad society has become through industrialisation and all the things we have done to make our lives easier. In these two pieces, one is from a novel and another is poetry, both written by the author Samuel Taylor Coleridge (see above). Both poems are talking about similar ideas with slight variations.

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
‘My Old Man!’ He said it so often. .
But he never stopped to think what
a terrible thing it was to say. It hurt us all.
And as time went on, we saw that he was getting thinner,
and smaller, and his eyes were more sunken in their sockets;
that the white hair had turned gray,
That his teeth became shaky when he spoke,
His knees shook with every step he took.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890

But then I looked around me and took heart again, because our men were already

author: robert_frost
text:
"He thought how very fine it would be if some one
Would give him an old coat and trousers of their own.
They were worn out, but they were clean; then why not
Have them? No one in his place had anything new—
Nothing! It must be fun for such as he to go about
Shining from head to foot, and having fresh clothes on
Every day. He had been thinking of that sort of thing ever since
The last man who worked here went away."

author: stephen_crane
text:
"This week has been a busy one for me;
And as usual I am tired out. To-night
There are four letters in my pigeon-hole;
Two of them came from Mary and Kate,
The others from you. One, which had no date
Was quite unintelligible to me.
I asked myself then if it were possible
That these three should be identical;
But since I found that they did not agree,
It seems evident enough that none of them
Is yours; so I put all into my box.

"It's nothing but good luck that we get
Him again this year. There'll be other days
When we shall need him. He does not know
That we are short of hands; and all he says
Is 'Why don't you employ me?' It goes on
The old way. I am always trying hard
To keep him down, as if I really cared
What he might want, or how he lived, or why,
Though for myself I hate these idlers best.
And yet he knows just enough about me

author: robert_frost
text:
"We are in town now; our friends come often here.
My boy has gone out and bought some things to sell,
And if you take them up into your bedroom, sir,
You may find one or two of those curious shells,
Which were brought from India and other lands,
For sale at an old woman's shop where they stand."

author: robert_frost
text:
"You know I haven't much, but I hope I may—

Well, thank you, sir. I do; I think so, too,
Because we live together here in love.
I never heard that a man should hate his wife.'"

author: stephen_crane
text:
There was once a lady who kept
a shop full of dolls, and she was very fond of dolls. She used
to talk about them all day long. The children at school began to
laugh behind her back because they thought it so odd to be always talking about things which had no life. But one day as she sat at home alone with her doll collection, there came up before her eyes a picture of the first time when she saw those great glass-eyed dolls standing on shelves beside her mother’s sewing table; the memory brought the old feeling of love and delight into her heart

author: stothert_james_a

text: A poet's wife was dying. She had been married for fifty years and there were five children alive. It came upon her suddenly. Her husband thought it was because she was so old and feeble. The first child, whom he loved above all others, wanted his mother to live; and as she was lying on the bed, not knowing anything about what was going on around her, the boy went up to her bedside, put one arm round her neck and the other arm over her shoulder and cried aloud: 'Mother! Don't die!' She opened her eyes and looked at the child

author: stephen_crane
text:
It was in 1792 on a bleak day.
The sun had been shining for some weeks.
On this particular day it poured down with rain.
An old beggarwoman sat at the corner of a street.
She held up her hands and prayed that someone might give her something.
A young boy stood beside her.
He didn't have anything either.
"Don't you be frightened," she whispered,
"the storm will soon blow over."

author: stephen_crane
text:
The wind was blowing up
 Into the sky,
 And then into me
 Was drawn a sigh;
 But I was thinking, as I lay there,
 That I would like a home somewhere else;
 It wouldn't be so hot there, no doubt.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
The world's great heart within me beats,

To call a thousand worlds from rest :
I am a living flame for thee,

My Love, and mine thy bosom nest :
From out the dark abysses deep
Of Being, we shall rise together,
In love, beyond the reach of sleep;
Where stars unnumbered meet their peer.

author: thomas_hardy
text: Let me not speak for him who cannot say : “ I am.”

We have, from Time’s beginning, dreamed and sung
The melody that thrills this living world :
We had not heard till now where all things hung
From one great heart-string which was made of cord.

O! there, at last, are we—those beings whose song
Was sung without us, but for whom it sang;
Our lost true selves once more together thronged
In harmony with all—with heaven itself.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
"He hath created man out of a drop of blood."

Thus the Prophet speaks; and we remember too,
How oft at morn, when first he wakes upon his bed,
The drops of dew are seen distilling from his head,
Like pearls to light beneath the morning sun.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
Earthly Love’s true centre we shall find;
Where all who are one love for a life
Of heart and soul and mind shall combine!

“For though there be none like unto thee”

author: thomas_hardy
text: I am too tired to speak or move!

author: william_wordsworth
text: THE morning air is soft and fair!

author: thomas_hardy
text: (The following is an extract) "And I've wandered, far away from home! Through many lands that seemed fair enough, But still it was not my native air— So back I came, to try to live alone."

author: thomas_hardy
text:
It was a time that is past,
 When men were just but not fast,
 Or wise but seldom crass;
 In fact they did the best
 That could be done, although
 With some degree of bluster.

 Then came an age of haste,
 Of feverish endeavor;
 Of thought too swift to last,
 Too quick, alas! To wait;
 So many things went wrong
 As never yet have gone right.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
I wish to-day could find
 Such words as none have found before,
 The music, which no voice has sounded,
 Which in your soul shall live for evermore.

author: buchanan_robert
text:
The Sun is set! The sun has sunk into his bed.
 He leaves us in darkness. He is gone for ever.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
Thou didst give birth, from thy green breast, to him.
 That nursed me, in his arms, when all was dim,
 And all were dark about us; taught me then,
 How to look up, and learn to breathe again,
 To hear and see what thou hast done for men!
 Thy hand hath drawn me through these years; thy light
 Hath shone upon me like an angel's face;
 And thou art still a mother, though at night
 She shuts her eyes, and leaves us sleeping-place
 Within her heart! Oh! never

author: william_wordsworth
text: I have long felt the necessity of forming in myself those ideas of the rights of man which would naturally produce an attachment for democracy. It has been impossible, however, so long as I lived under the British government, to give these principles any practical operation. The first step toward acquiring this knowledge was made when I removed from London to Glasgow; but even then I had no opportunity of applying it to practice until I was called upon to support the claims of American independence.
